query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermo‐mechanical processing that refines the eutectic lamellar microstructure into an ultrafine duplex structure can simultaneously enhance both the yield strength and ductility of eutectic high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g. AlCoCrFeNi2.1) exhibiting a coarse, inherited lamellar microstructure with moderate strength and limited ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply a single-step thermo-mechanical treatment combining controlled hot rolling with rapid annealing to induce dynamic recrystallization and refinement of the eutectic lamellae into an ultrafine duplex composite structure.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed at elevated temperatures using hot rolling followed by rapid annealing (e.g., short time at ~850 °C with a high heating rate) under conditions similar to those reported for in situ ultrafine-grain formation in EHEAs.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine duplex microstructure that preserves a refined version of the original lamellar architecture, manifesting hierarchical heterogeneity.
generation.mechanism: The refined duplex structure promotes a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a microcrack-arresting mechanism, which together enable increased dislocation interactions, enhanced yield strength, and improved strain redistribution, thereby simultaneously boosting strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the processed alloy is expected to exhibit a significant increase in yield strength (potentially on the order of 50% higher) alongside enhanced ductility, as the ultrafine duplex structure better accommodates plastic deformation.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy in the as-cast condition with coarse lamellar microstructure.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected for eutectic HEAs with similar compositions that can undergo the necessary phase transformation; deviations in alloy composition or processing parameters that hinder lamellar refinement may not yield the predicted enhancements.
generation.uncertainty: While the beneficial mechanism is supported by prior observations, the exact quantitative improvement in strength and ductility is sensitive to processing parameters; further optimization and broader compositional studies are needed to establish precise performance metrics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA samples: one group processed using the specified hot rolling plus rapid annealing protocol and one group left in the as-cast state. Perform tensile tests and microstructural characterization (e.g., using SEM/TEM) on both groups.
measurements: Grain size and lamellar spacing via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermo-mechanically treated samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both yield strength and ductility relative to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
